title: Getting Started with GitHub Pages
excerpt: A comprehensive guide on how to set up and deploy your own GitHub Pages site with custom domain and HTTPS.
content:
What is GitHub Pages?

GitHub Pages is a static site hosting service that takes HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files directly from a repository on GitHub and publishes them as a website.

Setting Up Your Site

To get started, create a repository named username.github.io. Any files you push to this repository will be served at https://username.github.io.

Custom Domain

You can also configure a custom domain for your GitHub Pages site. Simply create a CNAME record pointing to username.github.io and add your domain in the repository settings.

title: HTML & CSS Tips for Beginners
excerpt: Essential HTML and CSS tips that every web developer should know to build better, more maintainable websites.
content:
Use Semantic HTML

Semantic HTML elements like <header>, <nav>, <main>, and <footer> help screen readers and search engines understand your page structure.

CSS Flexbox & Grid

Modern CSS layout techniques like Flexbox and Grid make it much easier to create responsive layouts without relying on float-based hacks.

Keep It Accessible

Always add alt text to images, use sufficient color contrast, and ensure your site is navigable via keyboard.

title: Understanding JavaScript Async/Await
excerpt: A deep dive into JavaScript's async/await pattern, promises, and how to handle asynchronous operations effectively.
content:
Callbacks to Promises

JavaScript has evolved from callback-based asynchronous programming to promises, and now to async/await — the most readable approach.

Async/Await Basics

The async keyword declares an asynchronous function, while await pauses execution until a promise resolves.

async function fetchData() {
  const response = await fetch('/api/data');
  const data = await response.json();
  return data;
}

Error Handling

Use try/catch blocks with async/await for clean error handling:

async function getData() {
  try {
    const data = await fetchData();
    console.log(data);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Failed:', error);
  }
}

title: My Development Environment Setup
excerpt: A tour of my current development environment including editor setup, terminal configuration, and essential tools.
content:
Editor: VS Code

Visual Studio Code is my primary code editor. Here are my essential extensions:

  • GitLens — supercharged Git capabilities

Terminal

I use Windows Terminal with WSL2 (Ubuntu). My shell is zsh with Oh My Zsh and the Powerlevel10k theme.

Git Workflow

I follow a feature-branch workflow with conventional commits. This keeps the project history clean and makes collaboration easier.

title: CSS Grid vs Flexbox: When to Use What
excerpt: Understanding the differences between CSS Grid and Flexbox and knowing when to use each layout method.
content:
Flexbox: One-Dimensional Layout

Flexbox is designed for one-dimensional layouts — either a row OR a column. It's great for distributing space along a single axis.

Grid: Two-Dimensional Layout

CSS Grid is designed for two-dimensional layouts — rows AND columns simultaneously. It excels at creating complex page layouts.

When to Use What

Use Flexbox for: navigation bars, centering items, card rows, form elements.

Use Grid for: full page layouts, gallery grids, dashboard layouts, any layout needing both row and column control.
